Kurtis Olin sat in the recliner in his living room listening to Bach’s Brandenburg number 2 set to play in a repetitive loop. He had planned to do so much today, but instead he had spent most of the day playing games and watching old movies. What he hadn't planned on was being told that he only had a year to live. While the pains in his body had been getting worse, he never thought it had gotten that bad. Not critical anyway.

“What do you mean a year,” he had said to his doctor earlier. “Of course you can’t know that for sure! A year? I mean I feel perfectly fine.”

“You don’t feel fine,” said Dr Patel. “If you’re not lying to me, your're lying to yourself. Based on your test results, I would be able to know for sure that you’ve been having trouble breathing. Am I right?

Kurtis said nothing.

Perhaps some blurriness of vision? There would be dozens of other symptoms as well but you would have been getting used to them by now. Even now, if you just looked at yourself a mirror, it would be plain to see that something is very wrong.”

Kurtis looked at himself with a frown. His body was covered in black and purple marks. There was a discharge from his eyes and purple lines spider webbed all over his body in faintly visible lines as the radiation virus spread throughout his body. All he could think was, I do look like a man with less then a year to live.

“Well what can I do? Surely there’s something you can give me.”

“What I would advise you to do is what you’ve been advised to do for a year now, for ten years, hell; probably your entire life. Stay away from the radiation. Get proper rest. Exercise! But you haven’t and you won't. People like you never do and I’d just be wasting my time.”

Kurtis smoke up weakly. His voice barely carrying the weight of a feather. “I have a family doctor. Two kids. A wife.”

“And you have failed them. You knew what the risks of the radiation were. We all do. But you choose to keep exposing yourself to it. I’d suspect that your family has been exposed to it too am I right? Too a lethal extent?

“No! No!..." Kurtis grew indignant that the accusation, "I’d never allow my son to be exposed. And my other son is too young.”

Kurtis didn't mention his wife who, though much healthier, had the same spiderweb pattern tracing her own body.

“Children will often follow the examples of their parents Mr Olin. In the Late Twentieth century parents would talk to their children about not smoking till they were blue in the face then they themselves would turn around and ingest pack after pack of tobacco. Do you really think those children didn’t follow their parents actions rather than their words.”

“This is different.”

“What is your son’s exposure rate?”

“It’s under control,” shouted Kurtis defensively.

“Is it above normal?”

“Only a little. And only because he has trouble controlling himself. But whenever I’m around--”

“Mr Olin, you won't be around much longer. And once you're gone, your son will follow quickly behind you. Then his brother. I'm sure your wife will be gone long before either of them. You’ve not just killed yourself Kurtis. You’ve killed them too.”

The music reached it’s end and then started again. Kurtis looked down at his tablet where a calendar was displayed with tomorrow marked as day 365. Each progressive day counted down until the last day which was marked with only an X.

There was still time, he thought to himself. Still a little time.
